"""A readable guess at layer 15 MLP hidden unit 5698's write-out, as one rank-one component.

What the component is: one slice of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its activation is almost
entirely hidden unit 5698 of that MLP (weight 0.65), and it is small and diffuse: std 0.36 around
a mean of -0.05. Its value depends on long, mixed context, not on any one token. Current token,
previous token, position in the document, distance from the last newline and the model's own
surprisal together explain well under 1% of its variance.

What this program does: it predicts a flat baseline, with three readable adjustments that
follow its clearest behaviour.
  - The first token of each document is ~0 (it never fires there).
  - Chat-control tokens push it negative, most of all the closing think tag.
  - Newline tokens sit a little below the baseline.
Everything else gets the baseline. The adjustments are the only part with a visible pattern;
the bulk of its variance is left unexplained.
"""

READS = ()

BASELINE = -0.046
"""The component's typical activation (its mean over ordinary tokens)."""

CONTROL_TOKENS = {
    "</think>": -1.2,
    "<|im_start|>": -0.4,
    "<|im_end|>": -0.25,
    "<|endoftext|>": -0.1,
}
"""Chat-template control tokens and the mean activation each one gets."""

NEWLINE_VALUE = -0.11
"""Mean activation of a plain newline token."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_document = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if new_document:
        value = 0.0
    elif token in CONTROL_TOKENS:
        value = CONTROL_TOKENS[token]
    elif token.strip() == "" and "\n" in token:
        value = NEWLINE_VALUE
    else:
        value = BASELINE
    return carry, value

"""Explains layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 5699: a sparse feature that is near zero
almost everywhere and rises where a range or span has been opened and its end
("to", "until", "and", "through") is coming up.

What it does, in plain terms:
- A span is open when a start word ("from", "since", "between", "start", "starting",
  "begin", "beginning", ...) appears in the last few words with no closing word
  ("to", "until", "through", "and", "or") after it. E.g. "from the top right hand
  [corner]" expects " to"; "between 1911 [and]" expects its end.
- At clause boundaries (",", ".", "and", "or", "then") the feature rises more when a
  year, a month, or a start word has just appeared: "starting with 2023[,]",
  "from January 1, 2016[,]", "the first term is 2023[,]" fire most.
- On the last digit of a four-digit year (1800s-2000s), where a range end is likely
  next, it rises moderately.
- It goes clearly negative on "born" in a biography header ("Name (born"), and a
  little negative on "=" (assignments in code).

Only the text so far is read; each document starts fresh.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

BOUNDARY = {",", ".", "and", "or", "then"}
START_WORDS = {"start", "starts", "starting", "started", "begin", "begins", "beginning",
               "began", "first", "initial", "originally", "founded"}
OPENERS = {"from", "since", "between"} | START_WORDS
CLOSERS = {"to", "until", "through", "till", "and", "or"}
MONTHS = {"january", "february", "march", "april", "may", "june", "july", "august",
          "september", "october", "november", "december"}
YEAR = re.compile(r"[12]\d{3}")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[t]
    ts = prefix.token_strings
    # Look back at most 10 words, and only within this document.
    lo = t
    while lo > 0 and t - lo < 10 and prefix.document_ids[lo - 1] == doc:
        lo -= 1
    words = [s.strip().lower() for s in ts[lo:t]]
    cur = ts[t].strip().lower()

    if cur == "born":
        return carry, -3.5
    if cur == "=":
        return carry, -0.25

    # The last digit of a four-digit year.
    if cur.isdigit() and t >= 3:
        tail = "".join(s.strip() for s in ts[t - 3:t + 1])
        if YEAR.fullmatch(tail):
            return carry, 0.5

    # Is a span open? An opener in the last 8 words with no closer after it.
    last_open = max((i for i, w in enumerate(words[-8:]) if w in OPENERS), default=-1)
    last_close = max((i for i, w in enumerate(words[-8:]) if w in CLOSERS), default=-1)
    open_span = last_open >= 0 and last_open > last_close

    if cur in BOUNDARY:
        value = 0.25 + 0.1 * open_span
        if YEAR.search("".join(words)):
            value += 0.5
        if any(w in MONTHS for w in words):
            value += 0.4
        if any(w in START_WORDS for w in words):
            value += 1.3
        return carry, value

    return carry, (0.2 if open_span else -0.05)

"""Demonstrative words that point back at something just mentioned.

This component (layer 15, MLP down-projection, unit 5700) is a "demonstrative
pointer" detector. It is large on a demonstrative used as a determiner or pronoun
in ordinary prose: "This would certainly...", "In this way", "these figures",
"such acts", "during that period". Capitalised sentence-initial "This" and "These"
are the strongest. It is near zero on "this" in code ("this.name = x") and on
"that" used as a complementizer ("confirm that the error..."), which follows a verb
or adjective rather than a preposition. It also gives small values to same, similar
and above. Everything else is predicted as 0; the weak negative background on
quantifiers (other, several, many, all) is left out as too small to be worth a rule.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Typical activation on each pointer word, measured on sample text.
POINTER = {
    " This": 7.5, "This": 6.0, " this": 5.0, "this": 1.4,
    " These": 7.0, "These": 5.4, " these": 4.8,
    " Such": 6.2, " such": 2.5, " those": 3.0,
    " That": 5.3, "That": 4.6,
    " same": 0.9, " similar": 0.7, " above": 0.5, " latter": 0.7,
    " cette": 4.6, "该": 5.1, "这个": 4.5, "这": 3.6,
}

# "that" after a preposition or clause opener is a demonstrative ("during that period"),
# as after a verb of use or an adverb ("maybe that", "use that"). After a verb or
# adjective that takes a clause ("is that", "know that") it is a complementizer, ~0.
DEMONSTRATIVE_AFTER = set(
    "in on at for during since from by with of to into under over after before "
    "about through within upon if when because while but then maybe perhaps thus "
    "where how what once use compute take keep make put beyond around against "
    "though as wait later".split()
)
WEAK_AFTER_COMMA = {",": 2.8}
WEAK_AFTER_CONJUNCTION = set("so and than like or".split())

# Words before " this" that mark code, where "this" is a plain object reference.
CODE_BEFORE = {"", "=", "return", "(", "{", "[", "+", "&&", "||", "!", "->", "."}


def that_value(before: str) -> float:
    word = before.strip().lower()
    if word in DEMONSTRATIVE_AFTER:
        return 5.0
    if word in WEAK_AFTER_COMMA:
        return WEAK_AFTER_COMMA[word]
    if word in WEAK_AFTER_CONJUNCTION:
        return 1.5
    return 0.3


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2] if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if word == " that":
        return carry, that_value(before)
    if word in (" this", "this") and (before.strip() in CODE_BEFORE or before.startswith(("\n", "\t", " \n"))):
        return carry, 0.5
    return carry, float(POINTER.get(word, 0.0))

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 5701: a diffuse, context-driven signal with no
readable token rule. This program predicts 0 at every position.

What was checked on 8192 training rows (about 4.2M positions):
- Activation is roughly symmetric around 0 (std 0.32, mean ~0). Its sign and size
  vary within a document (97% of the variance is within-row).
- The current token alone explains ~0% of the variance (per-token means, held out).
- The previous token alone, the (previous, current) bigram, the token's character
  class (digits, spaces, punctuation, CJK, words) and window counts of those classes
  explain under 1.5% held out.
- Position in the packed row explains nothing; the first token of each document is
  about 0 and the second is slightly negative (mean -0.1), too small to matter.
- Activations are autocorrelated (lag 1: 0.30, lag 10: 0.07), so the signal is a
  slowly varying context property, not a token rule.
So the best simple prediction is 0, the component's mean. Switching it off changes
the model's output by almost nothing, consistent with that.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The component's activation is not predictable from the tokens seen so far.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5702: a negative response to dotted and slashed name pieces.

What it does: this component writes one direction into the residual stream. Its activation is
set largely by MLP hidden unit 5702 of layer 15 (that unit alone accounts for about 40% of its
variance). Typically it is small, within about +/-0.5, and it is large on a few tokens.
It goes clearly negative on a token that begins a name segment after a '.' or '/': a member
or qualified name such as `.name`, `.check`, `.Config` in code, or a path piece such as
`/tests`, `/model`. The largest negatives are attribute accesses in code. The largest
positives are separators inside package and file paths, which this simple version does not
capture.

Rule: predict -1.4 for a token that starts with '.' followed by a name (a dotted segment),
-0.8 for a token that starts with '/' followed by a name (a path segment), and 0 for every
other token. The values are the mean activations of those two groups on sampled text.

What it gets: about 5-7% of the activation variance on held-out rows (r about 0.26). Most
of the variance is per-token noise that surface features do not explain. Token identity alone
explains about 3% on held-out text, and the concepts I tried (previous token, line context,
path depth, copied tokens, the model's predicted next-token classes) add little on top. Switching
this program in for the component leaves the model's next-token predictions almost unchanged,
as switching the component off does.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

DOT_SEGMENT = -1.4
"""Mean activation of a '.name' token: a member or qualified-name segment."""

SLASH_SEGMENT = -0.8
"""Mean activation of a '/name' token: a path segment."""


def is_name_segment(token: str, sign: str) -> bool:
    """True if `token` is `sign` followed by at least one letter or digit."""
    return token.startswith(sign) and any(ch.isalnum() for ch in token)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if is_name_segment(token, "."):
        return carry, DOT_SEGMENT
    if is_name_segment(token, "/"):
        return carry, SLASH_SEGMENT
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP neuron 5703 (down_proj component 5703), as a readable predictor.

This component reads almost only the MLP hidden unit 5703 of layer 15 (its V vector is
dominated by that unit) and writes it into the residual stream with a small norm. Its
activation is a dense, roughly zero-centred signal (std about 0.3, values from -4 to +3.5)
that is almost unrelated to anything a short token-level rule can see: the current token
identity, the previous or next token, word/code/script classes, position in the document,
and short-window counts of such classes all explain about 0-2% of its variance. Its causal
importance is essentially zero, and switching it off changes the model's output by
about 1e-6 nats.

So the program only states the two things that are stable: the typical value (about
-0.047) at ordinary positions, and the nearly-zero value (about -0.007, almost no spread)
at the first token of each document, where the model resets its context.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL = -0.047  # mean activation at ordinary positions
DOCUMENT_START = -0.007  # activation at a document's first token (very tight around this)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    return carry, DOCUMENT_START if starts_document else TYPICAL

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5704: a "second thoughts" detector for reasoning text.

What it does: it reads the current token and predicts how strongly this component
writes into the residual stream there. The component is strongly positive on words
that turn a line of reasoning back on itself: "Wait", "Hmm", "Alternatively", "But",
"However", "Maybe", "Perhaps", "sure" in "Not sure", and question marks. It is mildly negative on
words that close an argument ("therefore", "so", "thus", "hence"), and most negative on
words that say a value is unspecified ("unknown", "arbitrary", "specify"). Everything
else is predicted as 0.

The weights are hand-set from the component's activation on sampled training text
(mean activation by word). A lookup of the word alone explains only a few percent of
the variance: most of the component's variance is small, context-dependent noise
spread across ordinary tokens, which this program does not model.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that reopen or doubt the line of reasoning: the strongest positive responses.
PIVOT = {
    "wait": 5.0,
    "hmm": 4.0,
    "alternatively": 3.5,
    "but": 1.5,
    "however": 1.5,
    "although": 1.5,
    "confusing": 1.5,
    "maybe": 1.3,
    "perhaps": 1.3,
    "confused": 1.2,
    "actually": 1.0,
    "sorry": 1.0,
    "though": 1.0,
}

# Words that close an argument: a small negative response.
CLOSE = {"therefore": -0.6, "hence": -0.6, "thus": -0.5, "so": -0.4}

# Words for an unspecified value: a stronger negative response.
UNSPECIFIED = {"unknown": -1.1, "arbitrary": -1.4, "specify": -1.0}

WEIGHTS = {**PIVOT, **CLOSE, **UNSPECIFIED}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if word == "sure":
        # "Not sure" is a strong doubt marker; "sure" elsewhere is not.
        previous = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
        return carry, (4.0 if previous == "not" else 0.0)
    if word.endswith("?"):
        # A question is an open doubt: a mild positive response.
        return carry, 0.8
    return carry, float(WEIGHTS.get(word, 0.0))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Demo: the predicted value for each word of a short reasoning snippet.
    text = "Wait, that is wrong. Hmm, maybe the answer is unknown. Therefore, not sure."
    for w in text.replace(",", " ").replace(".", " ").split():
        print(f"{w:>12} {WEIGHTS.get(w.lower(), 0.0):+.1f}")

"""Layer-15 MLP output component 5705: a closing-punctuation component.

What it does, in plain terms: it is quiet on ordinary words, and its sign and size
depend on the token that has just arrived.

- Strongly negative when a closing parenthesis runs straight into a maths operator,
  ")/", ")^", ")*", ")-" (as in "(x-5)^2" or "(3m+1)/2"): about -9.5.
- Negative on a space-then-closing-paren " )" (about -2.2), on a LaTeX "\\right"
  (about -3.4), and on an exponent digit right after "^" (the "2" in "x^2", about -1.8).
- Mildly negative on a plain closing ")", "]" or "}" (about -0.7 to -0.9), and on
  maths operators "^", "*", "/", "²" (about -0.3).
- Positive on closing quotation marks: a plain " or ” that ends a quotation is about
  +1.7; other quote characters about +0.1; emphasis that closes a bold or code span
  ("**", backtick) about +0.9.

Everything else is predicted as 0. The values are the mean activation of each group
on training rows, so the program reads as "maths-closing negative, quote-closing
positive". It explains only a small share of the variance: the component's large
swings depend on context that these token classes do not capture.

The program is stateless: each step looks only at the newest token and the one before
it (the one before is ignored at a document boundary).
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Quotation-mark characters that can close a quotation.
QUOTE_CHARS = re.compile(r'["”」』\']')
# Maths operators that can follow a closing parenthesis.
OPS = "^*/-"
# Bare maths operators.
MATH_OPS = {"^", "*", "/", "²"}
# Emphasis markers that close a bold or code span.
EMPHASIS = {"**", "`"}

# Mean activation of each group on training rows.
VALUES = {
    "close_paren_op": -9.5,    # ")/", ")^", ")*", ")-"
    "space_paren": -2.2,       # " )"
    "close_paren": -0.7,       # ")" and other ")..." tokens
    "close_bracket": -0.9,     # "]", "}"
    "latex_right": -3.4,       # "right" after "\"
    "exponent_digit": -1.8,    # digit right after "^"
    "emphasis": 0.9,           # "**", "`"
    "close_quote_hi": 1.7,     # a plain " or ” closing a quotation
    "close_quote": 0.1,        # other quotation-mark characters
    "math_op": -0.3,           # "^", "*", "/", "²"
    "other": 0.0,
}


def group(tok, prev):
    """Name the concept group of token `tok`, given the token before it (`prev`)."""
    t = tok.strip()
    if t.startswith(")") and any(c in t for c in OPS):
        return "close_paren_op"
    if tok == " )":
        return "space_paren"
    if t.startswith(")"):
        return "close_paren"
    if t.startswith(("]", "}")):
        return "close_bracket"
    if tok == "right" and prev.endswith("\\"):
        return "latex_right"
    if tok in EMPHASIS:
        return "emphasis"
    if tok in ('"', "”"):
        return "close_quote_hi"
    if QUOTE_CHARS.search(tok):
        return "close_quote"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d+", tok) and prev.endswith("^"):
        return "exponent_digit"
    if t in MATH_OPS:
        return "math_op"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Activation at the newest token: its group's mean value."""
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""
    return carry, VALUES[group(tok, prev)]

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5706: a weak, mostly unexplained readout.

What it does, plainly: this component's activation is a near-random, context-driven
number (typical size 0.4, no token or topic that predicts it). The one regularity we
could find is positional: right after a document starts, the activation dips
negative for about the first ten tokens, then settles to a small positive baseline.
This program predicts exactly that: a dip that fades with distance from the document
start, and the baseline elsewhere. It does not predict the bulk of the variance.
"""

READS = ()

BASELINE = 0.03  # typical activation once a document is underway
DIP = -0.14  # extra value at the 1st token after a document starts
FADE = 0.7  # the dip shrinks by this factor each token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids
    # distance from the start of the current document (0 at its first token)
    if carry is None or len(doc) == 1 or doc[-1] != doc[-2]:
        k = 0
    else:
        k = carry + 1
    if k == 0:
        return k, 0.0  # the first token of a document: activation is about zero
    return k, BASELINE + DIP * FADE ** (k - 1)

"""Layer 15, MLP down_proj, component 5707.

What it is: a rank-one piece of the layer-15 MLP down projection. Its input direction is
mostly (about three quarters of its norm) MLP hidden unit 5707, and that unit's value
correlates 0.56 with the component's activation, so the component is largely a read-out of
that one hidden unit.

What the program does: it has no trigger it can name. On about 4 million training tokens,
none of these explains the activation: token identity (unigram, bigram, and an additive
model over the last three tokens, all at or below 1.4 percent of variance on held-out
tokens), the character classes and word frequency of the current word, position in the
document, whether the token repeats an earlier one, and the density of garbled text in a
window. The largest activations are on specific words (negative on "is", "was", "be",
"health", "future"; positive on "user", "of", "data"), but each word's spread is about as
large as its mean. So the program predicts the component's mean activation everywhere, the
value that minimises squared error when nothing else is known.

Why it matters little: switching the component off changes the model's next-token
distribution by about 2e-6 nats per position, so it is a near-inert piece of the MLP.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.025
"""The component's average activation over the eval rows (mean -0.025, std 0.39)."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    return None, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 5708, read through this component (about 0.9 times that unit, plus
a small spread over other units). Its activation is a diffuse, context-dependent signal with
large tails both ways. Its typical value is about -0.03.

Checked on data, out of sample: the token's identity, the previous token, the token's
character class (word, digit, punctuation, space, CJK), whether the token repeats an earlier
one, and the position in the document each explain under 2% of its variance. Nothing
readable was found that predicts its sign or size.

One regularity: at the first token of each document the activation is essentially 0 (spread
about 0.007, against about 0.58 elsewhere). So the program predicts 0 there, and the typical
value everywhere else. This is a baseline, not an explanation of what the unit responds to.
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL_ACTIVATION = -0.03


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, TYPICAL_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP, component 5710 (down_proj), written out in plain terms.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection. Its input
direction is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 5710 of layer 15 (about a quarter of
its input-direction energy sits on that single unit), so its activation is that
unit's value scaled by about 0.3, plus small contributions from many other units.

What it does: the activation is a heavy-tailed, nearly symmetric signal around zero
(std about 0.32, rare excursions to +-4 to +-7). Nothing simple predicts it: token
identity, previous-token class, position, whether a token or bigram repeats earlier
text, the model's own entropy or confidence, and local character-class mix together
explain under 2% of its variance. So this program predicts the average value, and
only encodes the one thing that is exact: the first token of each document, where
the component is zero.

The program needs no state beyond the document labels; it reads only the newest token.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.027  # mean over the eval rows; the best constant guess


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids
    starts_document = len(doc) == 1 or doc[-1] != doc[-2]
    if starts_document:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Algebra-symbol reader for layer 15's MLP hidden unit 5711.

This component is mostly that single MLP hidden unit (unit 5711 carries about two-thirds of
its read direction), so its activation tracks that unit's value, scaled by about 1.2. The unit
is quiet on most text and its large values are mostly positive, and they come on the symbols of
algebra: the plus and minus signs, the variable x, a superscript ² or a caret, and the colon
that ends a line of worked math. It fires hardest on a plus or minus sign that comes within a
few tokens after an exponent (², ^), as in "x² + 2a x + a²". Its scatter is wide and mostly not
captured by any short rule. This program writes a fixed value for each such symbol, zero
elsewhere, and a larger one for signs that follow an exponent within the last 8 tokens of the
same document. It explains only a small share of the variance (about 0.4% on eval).
"""

READS = ()

EXPONENT = {"²", "³", "^", "**"}
# Typical activation for each symbol, with an exponent nearby or not.
SIGN_PLAIN = {"+": 0.75, "-": 0.17}
SIGN_AFTER_EXPONENT = {"+": 1.6, "-": 1.1}
OTHER = {"x": 0.4, "²": 0.2, "^": 0.2, ":": 0.3}
LOOKBACK = 8


def _recent(prefix, k):
    """The up-to-k tokens before the current one, from the same document, stripped."""
    t = prefix.position
    out = []
    for i in range(t - 1, max(-1, t - 1 - k), -1):
        if prefix.document_ids[i] != prefix.document_ids[t]:
            break
        out.append(prefix.token_strings[i].strip())
    return out


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if cur in SIGN_PLAIN:
        after_exponent = any(s in EXPONENT for s in _recent(prefix, LOOKBACK))
        table = SIGN_AFTER_EXPONENT if after_exponent else SIGN_PLAIN
        return carry, table[cur]
    return carry, OTHER.get(cur, 0.0)

"""Baseline: predict the component's average activation everywhere.

Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5712 is a rank-one piece of the
layer-15 MLP down projection. Its activation is a dense, diffuse, roughly Gaussian signal
(mean about 0.04, sd about 0.31) with no token, position, document or script pattern that
simple rules can capture. This program predicts the mean at every position.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.042


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 5713: a Chinese/Japanese text detector.

What it does: the component is near zero on English, code and ASCII punctuation, and
switches on in running Chinese or Japanese text. It is strongest on Japanese kana
(hiragana grammar such as particles, verb endings and auxiliaries) and on kanji words
mixed with kana. Single Chinese characters and multi-character words are moderately high.
Katakana loanword syllables are weak. Korean syllables and fragments of multi-byte
characters (U+FFFD) are weakly positive, and CJK punctuation (、。，) is negative.

How the program works: it looks only at the newest token, sorts it into a script class,
and predicts the mean activation measured for that class on training text. The values
are those class means. Nothing is carried between positions.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

HIRAGANA = regex.compile(r"^\p{Hiragana}+$")  # の, は, ます, ことが
KATAKANA = regex.compile(r"^[\p{Katakana}ー]+$")  # loanword syllables: ット, ング
KANJI = regex.compile(r"\p{Han}")  # Chinese characters, and kanji
KANA = regex.compile(r"[\p{Hiragana}\p{Katakana}]")
HANGUL = regex.compile(r"\p{Hangul}")  # Korean syllables
CJK_PUNCT = regex.compile(r"[　-〿＀-￯]")  # 、。，！「」 and fullwidth forms
BROKEN = "�"  # a fragment of a multi-byte character, split across tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if HIRAGANA.match(s):
        value = 3.7
    elif KATAKANA.match(s):
        value = 0.6
    elif KANJI.search(s):
        if KANA.search(s):
            value = 4.8  # kanji mixed with kana: an inflected Japanese word
        elif len(s) == 1:
            value = 2.6  # a single Chinese character
        else:
            value = 3.3  # a multi-character word
    elif HANGUL.search(s):
        value = 1.6
    elif BROKEN in s:
        value = 1.0
    elif CJK_PUNCT.search(s):
        value = -0.8
    else:
        value = -0.1
    return carry, value

"""Words that negate or set up a contrast or exclusion ("not", "than", "without", "unlike",
"instead of", "beyond", "non-", "despite", "except", "prevent", ...), in English and in other
languages, make the activation negative: the more a word sets up a departure from the usual
or standard, the more negative. The effect fades over the next few words of the same phrase,
where a small negative value lands on the function words that complete it ("out of the",
"unable to", "away from"). Comparatives themselves ("more", "higher") are about zero, and
"than" after "more", "less" or "greater" (a number usually follows) is weaker."""

# Strongest: exclusion and contrast words.

             " ohne", " sans", " без", " чем", " 比", "比", "非"}
# Negations.

            "'t", "’t", " nicht", " keine", " nie", " pas", " не", " Не", " niet", " não", " nem",
            "不", "没", "没有", "无", "未", "不是", "不要", "不会", "无法", "不能", "沒有"}
# Milder: words that set up a contrast, a substitute or an avoidance.
CONTRAST = {" instead", " rather", " versus", " vs", " compared", " except", " outside", " despite",
            " although", " Although", " even", " Even", " less", " longer", " avoid", " prevent",
            " reduce", " eliminate", " replace", " unable", " lacking", " refused", " fewer"}
NUMBER_LEAD = {" more", " less", " greater", " fewer", " More", " Less"}
FADE = 0.5

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        carry = None

"""Colon-introducing-a-value detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj, component 5715.

What the component responds to: colons. It is strong on a colon that introduces a
value or an elaboration in ordinary text ("Author:", "Published:", "Reporter:",
"email at:", "Expected to find ... instead:", "Test Suites:"), and weak or negative
on colons inside code, paths, URLs and literals ("Validator.java:434", "case 3:",
"{0: 9", "http:"). The first colon of a document is stronger than later ones. Every
other token gets 0: its activation there is small and has no simple pattern.

The program keeps two small pieces of state per document: how many colons came
before, and the text of the current line so far.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# A path, URL or code-like word right before the colon, e.g. "Validator.java" or "http".
CODE_BEFORE = re.compile(r"[^\s]*[./][^\s]*$|^https?$")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        colons, line = 0, ""
    else:
        colons, line = carry[1], carry[2]

    value = 0.0
    if ":" in token or "：" in token:
        # Base strength of a colon that introduces a value.
        value = 1.5
        if colons == 0:
            value += 1.0  # the first colon in the document is the strongest
        if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 and prefix.token_strings[-2].startswith(" "):
            value += 0.5  # a colon after a space-separated word, as in prose
        if "\n" in token:
            value -= 0.7  # ":\n" and ":\n\n" weaker than a plain ":"
        if CODE_BEFORE.search(line) or line[:1] in (" ", "\t"):
            value -= 1.0  # code, path, URL or indented line
        colons += 1

    # Update the current line: it restarts after a newline.
    line = (line + token).split("\n")[-1]
    return (doc, colons, line), value

"""Layer 15 MLP neuron 5716 (its down_proj component), read as a loop-counter detector.

The activation is mostly small noise around a slight negative baseline, with rare large
spikes. The spikes come from a few recognisable places, mostly in source code:

* a loop counter (i, j, k, n, row, ...) right after a semicolon: the variable being tested
  in a C-style loop condition, as in `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)`. The strongest spikes.
* other short names right after a semicolon, weaker.
* a short name right after an opening bracket or paren, as in `a[i]` or `f(i`. Weak.
* `err` right after a comma, as in Go's `x, err := f()`.
* the opening chat tags `<tool_call>` and `<tool_response>`.
* the closing tags `</tool_call>`, `</tool_response>` and `</think>` are slightly negative.

A context counts as code when at least 5% of the last 64 tokens of the same document
contain code punctuation (`; { } ==` and so on). Elsewhere the activation sits near a small
negative baseline. The program keeps no state: it reads only the prefix.

This explains only a small share of the variance (about 3% on eval): most of it is noise
that no token rule captures. A large token-identity table only reaches about 3% on held-out
data, and a bigram table about 7%, so the readable rules give up little of what tokens alone
can give.
"""

import re

READS = ()

WINDOW = 64
CODE_MARK = re.compile(r"[;{}]|==|->|!=|\)\s*:|</?\w+>|\bdef\b|\breturn\b")
LOOP_NAME = re.compile(r" ?(i|j|k|n|m|l|p|u|x|y|row|col|column|idx|index)")
SHORT_NAME = re.compile(r" ?[A-Za-z]{1,2}")
BRACKET_NAME = re.compile(r"[\[(] ?[a-z]{1,2}")
TOOL_OPEN = {"<tool_call>", "<tool_response>"}
TOOL_CLOSE = {"</tool_call>", "</tool_response>", "</think>"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    # Only the tokens of the current document count: the row packs several documents.
    same = [
        s for s, d in zip(prefix.token_strings[-WINDOW:], prefix.document_ids[-WINDOW:]) if d == doc
    ]
    cur = same[-1]
    prev = same[-2] if len(same) > 1 else ""
    code = len(same) > 3 and sum(bool(CODE_MARK.search(s)) for s in same) >= 0.05 * len(same)

    if code and prev.endswith(";") and LOOP_NAME.fullmatch(cur):
        value = 8.0  # loop-condition counter, as in `for (...; i < n; ...)`
    elif code and prev.endswith(";") and SHORT_NAME.fullmatch(cur):
        value = 3.0
    elif code and BRACKET_NAME.fullmatch(cur):
        value = 1.0  # index variable, as in `a[i]` or `f(i`
    elif prev == "," and cur == " err":
        value = 5.0  # Go's `x, err := f()`
    elif cur in TOOL_OPEN:
        value = 3.0
    elif cur in TOOL_CLOSE:
        value = -0.8
    elif code:
        value = -0.03
    else:
        value = -0.06
    return carry, value

Its activation is the MLP hidden state read along one direction. That direction is mostly
hidden unit 5717 itself (weight 0.34) plus thousands of small weights, so the activation is
a blur over many units. Nothing simple in the token stream explains it: the identity of the
current or previous token, its character class, the position in the document, and whether
the token repeats all explain well under 1% of its variance on held-out text.

So this program predicts only the little that is systematic, from each token and its place
in the document:
  * a document's first token: the activation is about 0 there;
  * its second token: a little above 0;
  * tokens 3 to 6 of a document: higher, about 0.08;
  * whitespace-only tokens: a little higher, about 0.055;
  * everything else: the typical value, 0.034.
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL = 0.034
WHITESPACE = 0.055
SECOND = 0.016
EARLY = 0.08


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label, position of the previous token within its document)
    label = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != label:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    carry = (label, pos)
    if pos == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    if pos == 1:
        return carry, SECOND
    if pos <= 5:
        return carry, EARLY
    text = prefix.token_bytes[-1].decode("utf-8", "replace")
    if text.strip() == "":
        return carry, WHITESPACE
    return carry, TYPICAL

"""Sentence-boundary signal of MLP down_proj component 5721 in layer 15 (weak and noisy).

In plain terms: the component is positive where a sentence or line has just ended. It is
strongest on a sentence-final mark (. ! ? and their Chinese forms 。！？). That value grows
with the number of words in the sentence just finished, so long declarative sentences score
higher than short fragments, and it is higher again when that sentence contained a digit
(numbers, measurements, statistics). A newline scores a smaller positive value. Every other
token sits near a small constant. Its tails are much wider than this rule: most of its
variance lies in tokens the rule treats as flat, so the rule explains only a few percent.

The state carried from token to token is the word count and digit flag of the current
sentence. Both reset at a sentence mark, a newline, and the start of each document.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

SENTENCE_END = re.compile(r"[.!?。！？]\s*$")
BOUNDARY = re.compile(r"[.!?。！？\n]")
WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]")
DIGIT = re.compile(r"\d")

BASE = 0.04  # typical value on ordinary tokens
NEWLINE_VALUE = 0.19  # a line break
SENTENCE_INTERCEPT = -0.2  # sentence end with no words counted
PER_WORD = 0.047  # added per word in the finished sentence
MAX_WORDS = 30  # the word count stops growing here
DIGIT_BONUS = 0.53  # added when the finished sentence has a digit


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_document = len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    words, has_digit = (0, False) if carry is None or new_document else carry

    if SENTENCE_END.search(token):
        value = SENTENCE_INTERCEPT + PER_WORD * min(words, MAX_WORDS)
        value += DIGIT_BONUS if has_digit else 0.0
    elif "\n" in token:
        value = NEWLINE_VALUE
    else:
        value = BASE

    if BOUNDARY.search(token):
        words, has_digit = 0, False
    else:
        words += 1 if WORD.search(token) else 0
        has_digit = has_digit or bool(DIGIT.search(token))
    return (words, has_digit), value

"""Component 5725 of layer 15's MLP down_proj, as a two-topic word detector.

The component is a readout of the layer-15 MLP hidden state, mostly of hidden unit 5725
(its V vector is about 0.88 on that unit, out of norm 1.40). Its activation is high on words
from two topics:
1. Numerical and scientific Python / MATLAB code: np, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, plt, pandas,
   pd, MATLAB, conda, DataFrame, subplot, sklearn (strongest), and array, matrix, polynomial,
   plot, FFT, eigen, regression (weaker).
2. US military, veterans and government affairs: Veteran(s), VA, military, army, Army, navy,
   soldier, troops, cavalry, PTSD, Defense, Corps, Congress, Treasury, President, Trump, Obama.

Read through the unembedding (a logit-lens check), its output direction promotes words of
the same two topics as next tokens (soldiers, military, matlab, repmat, linspace).

The program scores each token: a topic word gets its weight, digits and blank tokens get a
small negative value, and a decaying count of recent topic words carries the topic across the
next few tokens of the same passage. The count restarts at each document. Everything else
reads as near zero, which is about the unit's mean.
"""

READS = ()

SCIENCE_STRONG = {
    "np", "numpy", "scipy", "matplotlib", "plt", "pyplot", "pd", "pandas", "MATLAB", "Matlab",
    "matlab", "conda", "DataFrame", "subplot", "sklearn", "ndarray", "dtype", "NaN",
}
SCIENCE_WEAK = {
    "array", "arrays", "matrix", "Matrix", "polynomial", "plot", "FFT", "eigen", "regression",
    "roots", "legend", "linalg", "Python", "python", "Excel",
}
MILITARY_GOVERNMENT = {
    "Veteran", "Veterans", "veteran", "veterans", "Vet", "VA", "military", "army", "Army",
    "soldier", "soldiers", "navy", "Navy", "cavalry", "PTSD", "troops", "Defense", "Corps",
    "Treasury", "Congress", "President", "Trump", "Obama", "Pentagon", "Senate", "federal",
}
STRONG_WEIGHT = 9.4
WEAK_WEIGHT = 1.9
MILITARY_WEIGHT = 2.9
CONTEXT_WEIGHT = 0.9  # per unit of the decayed topic count
CONTEXT_CAP = 3.0
DECAY = 0.9
BLANK_OR_DIGIT = -0.14


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (decayed topic count, document id of the previous token), None at a row's start.
    count, last_doc = carry if carry is not None else (0.0, None)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if doc != last_doc:
        count = 0.0  # a new document starts: forget the topic
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    strong = word in SCIENCE_STRONG
    weak = word in SCIENCE_WEAK
    military = word in MILITARY_GOVERNMENT
    count = DECAY * count + (strong or weak or military)
    value = STRONG_WEIGHT * strong + WEAK_WEIGHT * weak + MILITARY_WEIGHT * military
    if word == "" or word.isdigit():
        value += BLANK_OR_DIGIT
    value += CONTEXT_WEIGHT * min(count, CONTEXT_CAP)
    return (count, doc), float(value)

The component reads mostly one MLP hidden unit, unit 5726 of layer 15 (about 57%
of its input weight's squared norm). Its activation is dense and context-driven:
token identity alone explains almost none of it. What it does have is a clear
negative response to file-system paths typed in shell commands and tool calls:

  - the first directory name after that slash is strongly negative, most of

  - a name right after an open parenthesis, the first argument of a call

found captured it, and a token-identity table tops out near 1.5% held out.

alone), written into the residual stream along a fixed direction. Its value is mostly near
zero, and goes clearly negative inside GUI and user-interface code and prose: button, click,

marks the current token, and the share of UI terms among the 64 tokens before it, within the
same document, gives a UI density. The prediction is a small constant, minus the density, and
a stronger drop when the current token is itself a UI term inside a UI-dense stretch.

latent state that the token text does not show. This program explains only a small share.

from collections import deque

UI_WORDS = re.compile(
    r"button|click|input|form|menu|dialog|combo|checkbox|textbox|textfield|widget|gui|\bui\b"
    r"|label|select|slider|window|listener|mouse|keyboard|panel|edit|field|option|choice"
    r"|scroll|toolbar|tab|submit|cancel|display|screen|page|user|press|grid|item|view|tk|swing"
    r"|frame|event|textarea|dropdown|icon|modal|popup|alert",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]

"""Indentation tokens in code: a new line's leading whitespace, read against the line above.

Leading whitespace at the start of a line tends to be high when it is deeper than the
previous line, most of all when the previous line opened a block (ended in `{` or `:`),
and low when it dedents. Chat-role tokens such as `assistant` run negative. Other tokens
predict 0.
"""
READS = ()

OPENS_BLOCK = {b"{": 3.8, b":": 2.5}  # deeper indent after these line endings
DEEPER = 1.0  # deeper indent after any other line ending
SAME = {b"{": 2.5, b";": 1.7}  # equal indent after these line endings
SAME_OTHER = 0.7
SHALLOWER = {b"{": -0.6, b":": -0.6}  # dedent after these line endings
SHALLOWER_OTHER = -0.2
ROLE_TOKEN = {b"assistant": -1.5}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        carry = {"doc": prefix.document_ids[-1], "width": 0, "content": False, "lead": 0,
                 "last": b"", "prev_lead": 0, "prev_last": b""}
    b = prefix.token_bytes[-1]
    value = 0.0
    head, *rest = b.split(b"\n")
    if head.strip() == b"" and head and not carry["content"]:
        # leading whitespace of a line: compare its width with the previous line's
        new = carry["width"] + len(head)
        end = carry["prev_last"]
        if new > carry["prev_lead"]:
            value = OPENS_BLOCK.get(end, DEEPER)
        elif new == carry["prev_lead"]:
            value = SAME.get(end, SAME_OTHER)
        else:
            value = SHALLOWER.get(end, SHALLOWER_OTHER)
        carry["width"] = new
    elif head.strip():
        if not carry["content"]:
            carry["lead"] = carry["width"]
        carry["content"] = True
        carry["last"] = head.rstrip()[-1:]
        value = ROLE_TOKEN.get(head.strip(), 0.0)
    if rest:
        # a newline ends the current line; the text after it starts the next one
        if carry["content"]:
            carry["prev_lead"] = carry["lead"]
            carry["prev_last"] = carry["last"]
        tail = rest[-1]
        carry.update(width=len(tail), content=bool(tail.strip()),
                     lead=len(tail) - len(tail.lstrip()),
                     last=tail.rstrip()[-1:] if tail.strip() else b"")
    return carry, value

recognisable places, always inside short lines of knowledge-base style text such as

  and about -6.5 when the line names a relation ("instance of", "member of sports team",
  "located in", ...). Third and later separators are near zero.
- On those lines a comma or colon right after a relation name is mildly negative.
- "of" that opens the name of an institution or a list ("Department of", "Board of",
  "list of", "National Register of") is positive.
- Mild positive for an opening quotation mark, and for "the" after a locative preposition
  ("in the", "into the").

training text. The program explains only a few percent of the variance: most of the
component's activity is spread over common tokens (commas, "the", "of") in contexts that no
short rule captures.

READS = ()

SEPARATORS = ("—", "->", "|")
RELATIONS = (
    "instance of", "member of", "country", "performer", "place of", "occupation", "genre",
    "owned by", "given name", "family name", "languages spoken", "located in", "director",
    "citizenship", "sports team", "participant of", "conflict",
)
INSTITUTIONS = {
    "list", "department", "ministry", "board", "school", "institute", "court", "register",
    "field", "college", "university", "office", "council", "committee",
}
LOCATIVES = {"in", "into", "on", "at", "to"}
QUOTES = {'"', "“", "`"}

SECOND_SEPARATOR = -4.0  # second separator on a short line, no relation named
SECOND_SEPARATOR_RELATION = -6.5  # same, when the line names a relation
RELATION_PUNCT = -1.6  # comma or colon after a relation name
INSTITUTION_OF = 1.9  # "of" after an institution or list noun
LOCATIVE_THE = 0.3  # "the" after in/into/on/at/to
OPENING_QUOTE = 0.3  # opening quotation mark
SHORT_LINE = 40  # tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    tok = prefix.token_strings[t]
    new_doc = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    text, n_tokens, n_separators = ("", 0, 0) if (carry is None or new_doc) else carry
    prev = "" if new_doc else prefix.token_strings[t - 1].strip().lower()
    is_separator = any(s in tok for s in SEPARATORS)
    relation = any(r in text.lower() for r in RELATIONS)
    value = 0.0
    if is_separator and n_separators == 1 and n_tokens < SHORT_LINE:
        value = SECOND_SEPARATOR_RELATION if relation else SECOND_SEPARATOR
    elif tok.strip() in (",", ":") and relation:
        value = RELATION_PUNCT
    elif tok == " of" and prev in INSTITUTIONS:
        value = INSTITUTION_OF
    elif tok == " the" and prev in LOCATIVES:
        value = LOCATIVE_THE
    elif tok.strip() in QUOTES:
        value = OPENING_QUOTE
    if "\n" in tok:
        carry = ("", 0, 0)
    else:
        carry = ((text + tok)[-200:], n_tokens + 1, n_separators + is_separator)
    return carry, value

The component is one gated MLP unit, silu(gate) * up on neuron 5759, scaled by about 1.
Its largest values are negative, and they fall on the keyword `if` (or `elif`) when it
opens a conditional in source code: at the start of a line, or inside code (for example
`if (x == 0)`, `if not data:`, `} else if (`). The same word in ordinary prose
("apologize if it", "as if", "Alternatively, if") is only weakly negative. Almost
everything else is near zero, and no simple rule finds the rest of its variance.

This program: the word `if`/`elif` gets -1.0 in code (it starts a line, or the last 32
tokens of its document are at least 10% code punctuation) and -0.3 in prose. Every other
token gets 0.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

CONDITIONAL_WORDS = {"if", "elif"}
CODE_PUNCTUATION = set(";(){}[]=<>&|+*/#$")
WINDOW = 32
CODE_SHARE = 0.1
IN_CODE = -1.0
IN_PROSE = -0.3


def _starts_line(prefix) -> bool:
    """True when the token before the newest one ends a line, is indentation, or is absent."""
    if len(prefix.token_strings) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return True
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    return "\n" in before or before.strip() == ""


def _code_share(prefix) -> float:
    """Share of the last WINDOW tokens of this document that are code punctuation."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    tokens = [
        tok
        for tok, d in zip(prefix.token_strings[-WINDOW:], prefix.document_ids[-WINDOW:])
        if d == doc
    ]
    hits = sum(1 for tok in tokens if any(ch in CODE_PUNCTUATION for ch in tok))
    return hits / len(tokens) if tokens else 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if word not in CONDITIONAL_WORDS:
        return carry, 0.0
    in_code = _starts_line(prefix) or _code_share(prefix) >= CODE_SHARE
    return carry, IN_CODE if in_code else IN_PROSE
